clinical_knowledge.topic: Major Depressive Disorder evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Major Depressive Disorder is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management for moderate-to-severe Major Depressive Disorder (PHQ-9 >=15) emphasizes combination treatment: initiation of a first-line SSRI antidepressant together with referral for evidence-based psychotherapy (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy), with close early follow-up to monitor treatment response and safety.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: profound sadness, loss of interest in hobbies, fatigue, and early morning awakening for 3 months with PHQ-9 score 18

Key HPI features: 38F presents with 3 months of persistent low mood and loss of interest in hobbies she used to enjoy, including gardening and her book club. Reports difficulty falling and staying asleep with early morning awakening around 4 AM, decreased appetite with an unintentional 8-pound weight loss, low energy, poor concentration at work, and feelings of guilt about being 'a burden' to her family. Denies any prior episodes of elevated mood, mania, or psychotic symptoms, and denies any thoughts of self-harm or suicide. She has never taken an antidepressant or seen a therapist before.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 76, BP 118/74, unintentional weight loss of 8 lbs over 3 months. Mental status exam: appears tired with mildly slowed psychomotor activity; downcast affect congruent with reported mood but full range; speech normal rate and volume; thought process linear and goal-directed without evidence of psychosis; no suicidal or homicidal ideation elicited on direct questioning; insight and judgment intact. PHQ-9 depression screen score: 18/27 (moderately severe depression). Baseline TSH and CBC ordered to exclude hypothyroidism and anemia as contributing/mimicking causes.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Major Depressive Disorder.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adjustment disorder with depressed mood without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any suicidal ideation or plan — requires immediate safety assessment.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis using DSM-5 criteria (SIGECAPS: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor changes, Suicidality) with at least 5 symptoms present for 2+ weeks, and exclude medical mimics (hypothyroidism, anemia, medication side effects) with baseline TSH and CBC.

Perform a structured suicide risk assessment at this and every follow-up visit, directly asking about ideation, intent, and plan, since untreated depression carries meaningful suicide risk even without an initial positive screen.

Initiate first-line pharmacotherapy with an SSRI (e.g., Escitalopram 10 mg PO daily or Sertraline 50 mg PO daily), counseling the patient that a full therapeutic response may take 4-6 weeks and that early side effects (nausea, jitteriness) often improve within the first 1-2 weeks.

Refer for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy or another evidence-based psychotherapy, since combining medication with psychotherapy is more effective than either alone for moderate-to-severe depression; schedule close follow-up in 1-2 weeks initially (then every 4 weeks) to reassess PHQ-9 score, side effects, and safety.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: How would you describe your mood, and have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?
Are you waking up early and unable to fall back asleep?

Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn't worth living?

history.answer: I have been feeling deeply sad, exhausted, and completely unmotivated for about three months now.
It started about three months ago and has been present almost every single day, lasting throughout the entire day.
There was no specific loss, breakup, or financial crisis that triggered it; it just gradually took over my life.
I completely lost interest in gardening and my book club, which were activities I used to love and look forward to.
I have trouble falling asleep, and I keep waking up around four in the morning unable to get back to sleep.
My appetite has dropped significantly, and I have lost about eight pounds without trying over the past three months.
I feel drained of energy constantly, and my concentration at work has become really poor.
I keep feeling guilty and like I am just being a heavy burden to my family.
I feel like my body and thoughts are moving in slow motion, like I am walking through molasses.
No, I do not want to die and I have never had thoughts of harming myself.
I have never attempted suicide or harmed myself in the past, and I have no plan whatsoever to do so.
My husband and my two children are my world, and they give me every reason to get better.
It has been very hard to keep up with my tasks at work, and I have been withdrawing from my friends.
No, I have never had periods where I felt abnormally energetic, needed very little sleep, or felt unusually euphoric.
No, I have never heard voices that were not there or seen things that others could not see.
I only have an occasional glass of wine, and I do not take sleeping pills or use any illicit drugs.
I have not had cold intolerance, constipation, neck swelling, or sudden hair thinning.
No, I have not been pregnant recently; my youngest child is eight years old.
I have never experienced an episode like this before, and I have never seen a counselor or taken antidepressants.
No one in my family has a history of depression, bipolar disorder, psychiatric hospitalizations, or suicide.
I suspect I might be dealing with depression, but I felt embarrassed to bring it up until now.
I'm terrified that my lack of focus means I'll lose my job and end up being a burden to my family.
I'm hoping you can check my blood to see if something physical is off and maybe give me something gentle to help me sleep through the night.
I have high blood pressure and mild cholesterol elevation.
I had my appendix removed when I was a teenager, but I have had no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril ten milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I work as an administrative assistant in an office and live with my husband and two school-aged children.
My father has high blood pressure, but there are no other significant medical conditions in my family.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, my last period was two weeks ago, and there is no chance of pregnancy.
